papers.title: Directional and geometric characteristics of breaking-wave whitecaps in a laboratory wave basin
papers.abstract: The directional characteristics of wave breaking are essential for understanding surface wave dynamics. However, the directional representation of breaking in spectral wave models remains poorly constrained by experimental observations. This study analyzes breaking waves using image processing of whitecaps to extract crest-normal directions and geometric properties. The lower boundary of each active whitecap was used as a proxy for the local breaking-wave crest, with the associated direction defined as normal to the estimated crest. Whitecaps were identified and tracked across multiple cases, and the distribution of their crest-normal directions was compared with the directional spectrum of the wave field. The results indicate that narrower spectral distributions are associated with more focused distributions of crest-normal directions, demonstrating a correspondence between wave directional spreading and the directional organization of breaking crests. Geometric analysis further indicates a power-law relationship between whitecap area and crest length, which warrants further investigation across a broader range of conditions. These findings provide insight into the relationship between breaking-crest geometry and the directional properties of the wave spectrum.

papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. What do the ocean surface and a swaying flag have in common? Both are deformable surfaces exhibiting chaotic motion when exposed to turbulent flows. Whether such motion is primarily driven by flow turbulence or by nonlinear dynamics intrinsic to the surface remains debated. papers.title: On Modelling the Scattering of Highly Nonlinear Transient Water Waves Due to Surface-Piercing Cylinder. Part I: Formulations and Verifications
papers.abstract: The presence of extreme ocean waves poses substantial threats to the safety of marine engineering applications and navigational activities. Accurate prediction of the nonlinear wave loads on offshore structures in large-diameter cylindrical configuration, such as monopile wind turbines and platform columns, requires a robust solution to the high-order wave diffraction problem. This paper introduces a novel, highly nonlinear time-domain numerical pseudo-spectrum model based on potential flow theory. By leveraging the Fredholm integral equation of the second kind and Legendre polynomials, a distinct efficient solver for computing the velocity potential on the cylinder surface and vertical velocity at free surface is developed. The present method is verified by comparing with a direct approach based on Fourier transform and established theoretical models for simulating the scattering of small steepness uniform waves. The convergence and computational efficiency of the present method is also demonstrated. The validation of the new model for simulating highly nonlinear transient water waves will be reported in Part II. The proposed model provides a powerful and efficient new framework for analyzing high-order nonlinear wave diffraction and hydrodynamic loads, with significant implications for both scientific research and the engineering design of coastal and offshore structures.

papers.title: Stability of inverse cascade in NLS Wave turbulence
papers.abstract: We study the stability of the inverse cascade in the 3D Nonlinear Schrodinger Wave Kinetic Equation (WKE) in the presence and absence of a condensate. Using theoretical arguments supported by numerical simulation, we show that, the Kolmogorov-Zakharov solution is stable with respect to small isotropic perturbations in the absence of a condensate. Conversely, introducing a condensate component leads to a growth of the condensate occupation and ultimately destabilizes the inverse cascade. The system then evolves towards a new steady-state whose properties depend on the condensate dissipation rate.

papers.title: Generation of extreme waves with flexible features in fully nonlinear wave models
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. We consider the generation of extreme waves of flexible features in deep-water surface gravity waves, in the context of the fully nonlinear wave model, i.e. Euler equations of the free surface. This is achieved through a recently developed GenWave approach, coupled with the high-order spectral method to solve the Euler equations. Through an iterative refinement procedure, GenWave progressively refines the initial phases associated with a given wave spectrum, which leads to extreme-wave generation at specified design time and location, with their probability of exceedance quantified. In this study, we consider two types of extreme waves, enabled by the flexibility of GenWave. The first type is a spatially and temporally localised rogue wave, and second is a spatially localised extreme-wave group propagating at a constant speed. The two generated extreme-wave profiles are compared with their prototypes – the Peregrine soliton and regular soliton (or bright soliton) in the context of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS), with reasonable agreement. For the persistent group, comparison with linear evolution and the NLS identifies nonlinear persistence, faster propagation and bound-wave content beyond the leading-order NLS description.

papers.title: Decadal wave reconstruction in the Mediterranean Sea with graph neural networks
papers.abstract: Accurate simulation and prediction of ocean waves are essential for coastal risk management and climate studies. Deep learning has shown promising results for wave modeling, but most approaches still operate on regular grids and on forecasting time scales, and do not generalize to unstructured discretization or to long time horizons. Here we present WaveGraph, a model based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that emulates basin-scale wave dynamics directly on unstructured meshes with high resolution along the coasts (up to 2-3 km). Trained on bias-corrected simulation data over the Mediterranean Sea, WaveGraph uses a multiscale architecture combining the unstructured model mesh with a uniform graph, allowing simultaneous representation of local coastal interactions and large-scale wave dynamics. papers.abstract: The aim of this article is to derive a stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations, based on the location uncertainty principle (LU). papers.title: Surface gravity wave-mean flow interaction with comparable spatial scales. Part II: two-way coupling and wave-wave interactions
papers.abstract: We consider narrow-band deep-water surface gravity waves propagating above a background flow whose spatial scale is comparable to the wavelength. We focus on the regime where the background-flow speed is comparable to the Stokes drift of the waves to derive a two-way coupled model between the fast waves and the slow background flow. Nonlinear wave interactions arise at the same asymptotic order as the two-way coupling and must therefore be included in the derivation. The resulting model consists of a nonlinear version of the reduced wave equation obtained in part I, coupled to a Craik-Leibovich equation governing the evolution of the background flow. The model describes the evolution of the wave field and background flow over the slow turnover frequency of the background flow, thus saving the computational burden of temporally resolving the fast wave frequency. The inviscid model exactly conserves wave action, mechanical energy and horizontal momentum, while the viscous model exactly conserves horizontal momentum. The coupling terms are cast in compact form for ease of physical interpretation and numerical implementation.

papers.title: Monsoon‐Driven Wave–Current Interactions in the Arabian Sea Great Whirl: Wave Footprints Observed by SWOT/CFOSAT and Simulated by SWAN
papers.abstract: The Arabian Sea Great Whirl (GW) is a large, quasi‐stationary anticyclonic eddy that develops under the southwest monsoon, combining strong surface‐current shear with an energetic and seasonally organized wavefield. This setting provides a distinctive natural laboratory for examining wave–current interactions beyond the transient mid‐latitude regimes emphasized in previous work. Here we ask whether the GW produces a coherent and observable significant‐wave‐height (SWH) footprint, how the relative orientation of waves and currents controls its asymmetry, and how monsoon wind forcing regulates the relative importance of wind‐driven wave growth and current‐induced modulation. We combine multi‐satellite observations with SWAN (Simulating Waves Nearshore) numerical simulations to address these questions. The GW exhibits an asymmetric SWH pattern, with lower SWH where waves and currents align and higher SWH where they oppose, consistent with current‐induced refraction and wave‐energy redistribution. Wave–current modulation strengthens when eddy‐current gradients dominate the background wavefield, while stronger wind‐wave growth diminishes the current signature. Multiscale spectral analysis reveals scale‐dependent redistribution of SWH variability over the resolvable mesoscale range. papers.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
papers.abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

papers.title: On the spectra of strong turbulence on water surfaces
papers.abstract: Here, I give a brief history of the theory, with twists and turns, and list possible predictions for the spectra of the direct cascade of gravity waves on the water. The description of long waves is straightforward within the weak-turbulence theory developed by Zakharov and his school. As the energy cascade proceeds to shorter scales, the mean surface steepness grows, and wave-breaking events appear with increasing frequency. Considering surface cusps, Phillips suggested a wavenumber spectrum (with a wrong magnitude, as I argue here) and a frequency spectrum whose whole form is incorrect. The right form for the frequency spectral slope due to breaking waves was suggested by Kuznetsov. Here we estimate the magnitude and argue that the frequency spectrum is expected to continue unchanged through the whole cascade. The transition from weak to strong turbulence in the wavenumber and spatio-temporal spectra is due to spectrally nonlocal interactions and happens earlier (at larger scales) than the dimensional estimate suggests. As a result, the magnitude of the strong-turbulence spectrum is not universal but depends on the pumping for a sufficiently long weak-turbulence cascade. The reason for nonlocality is likely that breaking of shorter waves is determined by the magnitude of the longest wave on whose crest they are running.

papers.venue: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.abstract: This study is the first of a two-part paper that summarizes the development of a prototype coastal hazard prediction system providing short-term (+48 h) forecasts of the total water level (TWL) at 50 m resolution for the province of Quebec, Eastern Canada. In this first part, the implementation of the offshore wave model component of the system, which is a regional 1 km-resolution WAVEWATCH III™ (WW3) configuration for the Estuary and Gulf of St. Lawrence (EGSL), is presented and discussed. The configuration is forced by high resolution atmosphere, ocean and sea ice forecasts provided by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) and includes a state-of-the-art parameterization of wave propagation and attenuation in sea ice that has been tuned with observations from the EGSL. Performances are assessed against wave data collected over a 2-year period during which the forecasting system was running operationally, and against historical storm data using a model hindcast. Results demonstrate reasonable forecast skills both for normal and extreme wave conditions during ice-free periods with errors ranging from 15 % to 31 % of the mean wave height. However, when sea ice is present, performances are drastically reduced, primarily due to inaccuracies in the predicted ice fields at spatial scales over which wave energy typically dissipates in sea ice.

papers.title: Asymmetric Periodic Water Waves in Finite Depth
papers.abstract: We consider the full two-dimensional water-wave equations in finite depth, with and without surface tension. Water waves have been studied mathematically for more than two centuries. Reflection symmetry remains a common assumption in constructions of periodic steady waves, although asymmetric profiles have been observed in experiments and numerical computations. We construct families of periodic stationary solutions whose free surfaces have no axis of reflection, in both the pure-gravity and capillary--gravity cases. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first rigorous construction of asymmetric periodic pure-gravity waves for the full two-dimensional water-wave problem in finite depth. The proof combines localized vorticity laws with a Lyapunov--Schmidt reduction. In the pure-gravity case, we introduce a small background shear flow to obtain an invertible boundary operator and couple the interior and free-surface approximations at leading order.

papers.abstract: Wave breaking plays a central role in ocean dynamics, dissipating wave energy and shaping the evolution of the sea surface. papers.title: Sequential water wave reconstruction in VOF-based numerical wave tanks with the EnKF approach
papers.venue: Journal of Ocean Engineering and Science
papers.abstract: Existing phase-resolved wave reconstruction methods primarily rely on potential flow theory, which severely limits their capacity to capture strongly nonlinear phenomena such as wave breaking dynamics. To resolve this bottleneck, this study develops a robust sequential multiphase data assimilation framework integrating the EnKF with a VOF-based CFD solver. A key feature is a two-way phase representation conversion that maps the discontinuous native VOF field into a smooth level set signed distance field before assimilation, enhancing modal basis compactness and suppressing unphysical numerical oscillations. Multivariate POD is then applied to the joint ensemble of smooth interface and velocity fields, compressing the high-dimensional state space into a low-dimensional subspace with unified modal coefficients that naturally preserve cross-variable physical coupling and kinematic consistency. To mitigate ensemble collapse under repeated sparse observations, the relaxation to prior perturbations inflation method is embedded in the reduced-order coefficient space, using CFD-validated prior kinematics as a physical anchor to sustain sample diversity along physically consistent trajectories. The framework is validated via twin experiments across three representative wave conditions: fifth-order Stokes waves, JONSWAP irregular waves, and extreme plunging breakers on a shoaling slope.

papers.title: Renormalized quasi-resonant transport in surface-wave turbulence
papers.abstract: A renormalized coarse-grained transport formulation is developed for finite surface-wave turbulence in logarithmic frequency space. Shell elimination generates a running nonlinear activity on a restricted quasi-resonant channel whose frequency width is set by the nonlinear linewidth, while physical stationarity is imposed on the shell energy current rather than on the coupling itself. Microscopic Hamiltonian homogeneity together with constant flux fixes the underlying weak-turbulence scaling class and reproduces the classical capillary and gravity Kolmogorov–Zakharov spectra independently of the renormalization group (RG), providing its asymptotic consistency benchmark. The Wilsonian flow instead supplies the finite coarse-grained kinetics: it determines whether the corresponding stationary-current trajectory can be dynamically supported, how its effective coupling and linewidth run, and where the stationary weak branch loses validity. In squared-steepness variables, this exposes two distinct realizations: capillary transport follows a genuinely running trajectory, whereas deep-water gravity is the marginal scale-independent case, coinciding with fixed coupling in the ideal RG-supported interior.

papers.title: Scale effects on wave forces and flow structures around a perforated semicircular submerged breakwater
papers.abstract: Perforated semicircular submerged breakwaters can attenuate incident waves while allowing water exchange, making them suitable for coastal protection and marine infrastructure. Their hydraulic performance is often assessed using physical models based on Froude similarity, for which Reynolds similarity cannot be preserved. Extrapolating wave loads from reduced models to prototype conditions may therefore introduce bias. To quantify this effect, a validated numerical wave flume was used to examine six geometric scale ratios ( λ L = 1, 5, 10, 15, 25, and 35), four perforation rates ( ϵ = 0–15%), and five wave conditions. Validation used measurements from physical model experiments and field pressures obtained at prototype scale. Comparisons considered horizontal force coefficients, free surface elevations, velocity fields, and vorticity fields. Smaller models increasingly overestimated the shoreward peak force. At λ L = 35 and ϵ = 10%, the mean model to prototype ratio of the shoreward peak force coefficient reached 1.23. The differences between model and prototype responses were mainly associated with changes in wave transmission, reverse flow, and vortical motion over and behind the structure as scale decreased. These findings improve the interpretation of reduced model results and support more reliable prototype extrapolation of wave loads on perforated submerged structures.

papers.title: A parametric Morison-inspired model for wave-induced torque fluctuations on a vertical axis tidal turbine
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of surface waves on the hydrodynamic torque fluctuations of vertical axis tidal turbines. Wave-induced orbital velocities and accelerations are shown to generate periodic variations of the incoming flow, leading to significant unsteady torque loads. A reduced-order torque model inspired by Morison-type formulations is here developed to study wave-induced effects on vertical axis tidal turbines. The model is derived and expressed in terms of the instantaneous wave-modified tip-speed ratio and decomposes the torque response into three main parameters: a mean shift term, a linear sensitivity coefficient linking torque fluctuations to tip-speed ratio variations and an inertial coefficient proportional to the orbital acceleration. Phase-averaged analysis reveals the relative importance of velocity-driven and acceleration-driven mechanisms and the wave-induced torque variability is interpreted as a structured perturbation of the stationary performance curve. The results obtained under irregular waves demonstrate that the proposed Morison-type model is able to reproduce the wave-induced contribution to torque fluctuations with a limited number of parameters identified in monochromatic waves. The use of conservative coefficients derived from monochromatic wave tests appears as a promising strategy to bound torque fluctuations under a given sea state.

papers.abstract: In this paper, the nonlinear wave dynamics of the (3+1)-dimensional P-type model are investigated using a symbolic neural-network-based hybrid technique. The model is considered in the context of nonlinear wave propagation, which is of practical importance in different areas. This approach combines the modified generalized Riccati equation mapping method with a neural network structure, where each neuron in the first hidden layer represents a Riccati-based activation function, which allows the construction of new physics-based trial solutions. This approach allows the systematic generation of exact traveling wave solutions in space and time. Solutions including solitary waves, and periodic and localized pulses are obtained, which provide essential insight into the influence of model parameters on wave profiles and evolution in complex media. The dynamics of the waves are illustrated by two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and contour plots, which show the behavior of propagation, localization, and stability. The results demonstrate the method is feasible, efficient, and effective for studying high-dimensional nonlinear systems. This work not only extends the Riccati-based neural network approach to the model but also provides a platform for exploring nonlinear wave behavior in shallow-water flows and other hydraulic engineering problems.

papers.title: Turbulent mixing by non-breaking surface waves in the ocean: theory, observation and modeling
papers.abstract: Most ocean general-circulation models face the persistent challenge that the simulated summer ocean mixed layers are too shallow, indicating a lack of mixing; climate models coupled to them simulate too hot sea-surface temperatures (SSTs). Global wind energy input to the oceans supplies a great amount of energy to the surface waves. It is commonly thought that wave-induced turbulence mixing occurs only through wave breaking, but that turbulence, though intense, is injected only to a depth of the order of a wave height. Here we lay the theoretical foundation that non-breaking ocean surface waves can enhance background turbulence and increase irreversible mixing. Such turbulence dissipation and mixing extend to about a horizontal wavelength in depth, comparable to the mixed-layer depth. The direct wave-to-turbulence transfer of energy occurs without needing to be linked to the second-order Stokes drift, and mixing is thus more effective. When introduced into ocean models, such mixing effectively reduces model biases, producing deeper summer mixed layers and cooler SSTs where waves are stronger, as in observations. The predicted wave-turbulence interactions have characteristics which are consistent with laboratory and field observations, including the wave-modulation of turbulence as an energy transfer mechanism, and absence of phase locking to the wave.

papers.venue: Journal of Ocean Engineering and Science
papers.abstract: The development of Oscillating Water Column (OWC) devices is hindered by a critical gap in understanding: the neglect of coupling effects between key parameters in the estimation of energy conversion efficiency. This study introduces a novel experimental framework to address this issue. Through a comprehensive campaign of laboratory tests encompassing 345 operational conditions, the influence of several key parameters is investigated: Power-Take-Off (PTO) damping, chamber geometry and wave characteristics. For the first time, a method is developed for estimating the efficiency ( ξ ) under irregular waves that explicitly accounts for complex parameter interactions. The results unequivocally reveal strong coupling effects. For instance, the influence of the internal water depth is amplified with a greater chamber length, and the impact of the front wall draft diminishes as the relative wavelength increases. Crucially, it is found that neglecting these coupling effects leads to significant errors (of up to 58%) in estimating the efficiency. The proposed method achieves excellent accuracy (R 2 =0.96) in predicting efficiency across complex parameter variations. Advancing beyond the conventional, isolated analysis towards a coupled perspective, this research establishes a validated framework for the selection of the optimal parameter space for OWC devices.

papers.title: Freeze, Then Select: Structured Field Adapters and Stability-Validated Weak Selection for PDE Discovery from Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: PDE discovery from sparse observations requires reconstructing a continuous field and selecting the correct differential terms. Our analysis of optimization paths in coupled neural PDE discovery reveals three behaviors: the exact support can persist to the end of training, appear only transiently, or fail to emerge. To decouple equation selection from neural optimization, we develop a freeze-then-select method combining a structured field adapter with Stability-Validated Weak Selection (SVWS). Trained from observations without a PDE residual, the adapter factorizes the field into learned spatial features and temporal coefficients represented by cubic splines. After freezing the field, SVWS identifies recurrent terms across independent weak-form systems, refits candidate supports, and selects the final equation on held-out weak-form systems. Beyond fixed libraries, we apply the same principle to expressions generated by genetic programming and recover the power-law form of an unknown nonlinear diffusion function from sparse, noisy observations. Across all six sparse MDBench regimes, our method attains the highest exact support recovery rate, with its clearest gains over classical and neural baselines on challenging Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics.

papers.title: Towards conditional low-frequency response design waves for floating offshore wind turbine applications
papers.abstract: Traditional stochastic sea-keeping analysis for floating wind turbines requires long-duration simulations to capture the extreme surge platform response and mooring line loads. This work explores methods to condition short-duration design waves that induce an extreme low-frequency surge offset, due to both difference-frequency wave forcing and aerodynamic thrust loads from a constant mean wind-speed, with the aim to facilitate more detailed numerical, or physical, analysis of the extreme responses experienced by floating wind turbines. Two methods of conditional target are considered: analytical maximum response, and a most-likely extreme response ‘profile’. The conditioning approach relies upon a fast single degree-of-freedom frequency-domain model, which is shown to compare reasonably against a time-domain diffraction-radiation model. Both conditioning methods are capable of inducing the target response, and within short durations, down to a single surge natural period. Whilst the inclusion of a mean wind load is demonstrated, further work is necessary to extend the applicability to turbulent wind loads, which may be significant.

papers.title: Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine: A Scientific Agent for PDE Discovery with Unknown Spatial Coefficient Fields
papers.abstract: Discovering PDEs in heterogeneous media requires jointly identifying the governing operator and the unknown spatial fields that parameterize it. These tasks are coupled: changing field placement changes the differential law, while a sufficiently flexible field can conceal structural error on a single trajectory. We present Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine for PDE Discovery (HER-PDE), a scientific-agent framework that discovers compositional PDE structure together with nonparametric, time-invariant coefficient fields. The Agent analyzes two noisy trajectories generated by different excitations, proposes complete expression-tree hypotheses, and combines creative structural exploration with local candidate refinement. Its Hypothesis Evaluation Interface (HEI) estimates only the fields explicitly declared in each hypothesis, never adds missing terms, and scores structures by bidirectional cross-excitation transfer. The selected law is subsequently audited on a sealed temporal interval. Across five controlled two-dimensional systems observed with 5 percent relative Gaussian state noise, the Agent recovers the generating operator in all five cases, including equivalent signed-field and product-rule parameterizations. Across nine unknown coefficient fields, the recovered fields attain a median Pearson correlation of approximately 0.85 and a median relative L2 error of approximately 0.28.

papers.title: On the post-hoc Evaluation of PDE Discovery: A Multifaceted Challenge of Scientific Advancement
papers.abstract: PDE discovery aims to identify from data the governing law of a physical system. Constituting a cornerstone of scientific advancement, it has become during the past decade a major line of research in the rapidly evolving field of Physics-informed Machine Learning (PiML). Among the open problems to address in this domain, the post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs raises the particular difficulty of being multifaceted. Indeed, it requires jointly considering predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization capacity, some of these properties being conflicting. Drawing on an extensive body of literature spanning ML, numerical analysis and symbolic regression, we establish in this article that the overwhelming majority of papers address only certain aspects of the overall evaluation task. To better understand their limitations when used in isolation from the others, we propose the first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics. Through experiments conducted on several PDEs, we observe that limiting the scope of the evaluation can lead to overstated conclusions as well as changes in the ranking of the identified equations. papers.abstract: Coastal tidal dynamics play a crucial role in a variety of biogeophysical processes, ranging from compound flooding to sediment transport. Satellite altimetry has revolutionized our understanding of ocean tides, but coastal regions remain challenging for satellite altimetry-based observations. In recent years, important efforts have been made to produce shoreline measurements from satellite optical imagery. These datasets raise the question of whether shoreline observations can resolve tidal dynamics at fine coastal scales. Here, we show that shoreline measurements provide fine-scale insights into tidal characteristics, demonstrating variability at beach scales across the Pacific Rim. We explore how both harmonic analysis and response-based methods can be applied to these data to study a range of tidal constituents. Our results are contrasted with in situ measurements and state-of-the-art models as well as with wide-swath satellite observations. We demonstrate that satellite-derived shoreline measurements are a valuable resource for tidal research, particularly for model validation and the study of tidal constituent variability in the coastal zone. Satellite-derived shoreline measurements can provide insights into coastal tidal dynamics and for the validation of models in the coastal zone, according to analyses using shoreline position data from around the Pacific Rim.

papers.abstract: The finite span and twist of wind turbine blades induce spanwise flow, along with a tip vortex. Conventional blade element theory, rooted in a two-dimensional assumption, cannot capture these spanwise effects. The model captures two fundamental phenomena: downwash that modifies the local effective angle of attack and tip pressure loss driven by radial velocity transport. A coherent physical pathway from the tip vortex to load reduction is established: the spanwise flow transports energy from the tip element into the tip vortex, reducing suction-side velocity and thereby weakening suction at the equivalent angle of attack. Furthermore, symbolic regression is then used to determine two unknown velocity factors from limited experimental data, serving as closure terms.
